fields.definition: The perceived left-to-right spatial spread of a choir within a stereo image, set by microphone technique, singer placement, and the panning of section spot mics.
fields.plain_english: How wide a recorded choir sounds from your left speaker to your right. A wide choir seems to fill the room; a narrow one sounds squeezed into the middle.
fields.purpose_function: Width spreads the voice sections across the stereo field so listeners can sense the size and layout of the group, adding a feeling of space.
fields.practical_application: An engineer sets choir width by choosing a spaced or coincident mic pair and by panning section spot mics, widening or narrowing the group to fit the mix.
common_mistakes: Panning section mics too hard, leaving a hole in the middle of the choir
Assuming wider always sounds better, when too much width can smear the blend
Confusing width with depth; front-to-back space is depth, not width
scenario_contexts: Recording a concert choir with a spaced pair to capture a wide, natural spread
Narrowing choir width so the group sits behind a solo vocalist
Setting up a main pair and outriggers over a choir in a hall

fields.definition: The way choral singers attack, sustain, and release notes and consonants, such as legato, staccato, or marcato, which shapes how connected or detached the sung line is.
fields.plain_english: How a choir starts, holds, and ends each note and word. Smooth singing joins notes together; crisp singing separates them, like gliding versus tapping.
fields.purpose_function: Articulation gives a choral line its rhythmic clarity and musical character, letting a group phrase together and match the style of the piece.
fields.practical_application: A recordist captures articulation by miking for consonant detail and clean transients, while the director marks legato or staccato passages to unify the ensemble.
common_mistakes: Smearing crisp articulation with heavy reverb
Confusing articulation with dynamics; one is note shape, the other is loudness
Miking so far back that consonant attacks get lost
scenario_contexts: Capturing crisp consonant attacks in a rhythmic choral passage
Recording a legato hymn where notes must flow smoothly
Adjusting mic distance to keep staccato singing tight and clear

sources: Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians

fields.definition: The amount of high-frequency energy and treble presence in a choir's sound, which makes voices sound clear and open rather than dark or muffled.
fields.plain_english: How bright or crisp a choir sounds in its high tones. A bright choir sounds clear and sparkly; a dull one sounds soft and covered.
fields.purpose_function: Brightness helps a choir cut through a mix and keeps words and overtones clear, though too much can sound harsh or sibilant.
fields.practical_application: An engineer shapes brightness with mic choice, mic placement, and EQ, boosting highs for air or cutting them to tame harshness.
common_mistakes: Boosting high EQ too much, which makes sopranos harsh and sibilant
Blaming a dull choir on the mic when the room or placement is the real cause
Confusing brightness with loudness
scenario_contexts: Adding a gentle high shelf to open up a choir recorded in a dark hall
Choosing a condenser mic with an airy top end for a chamber choir
Cutting harsh highs when close-miking sopranos

fields.definition: How thick or full a choral texture sounds, set by the number of voices, how many notes are stacked, and how the parts are voiced and doubled.
fields.plain_english: How full and thick a choir sounds. Many singers on many notes feel dense and rich; a few voices on simple lines feel thin and open.
fields.purpose_function: Density controls the weight and richness of a choral arrangement, helping a section feel powerful or leave room for other parts.
fields.practical_application: An arranger adjusts density by adding or removing voice parts and doublings, while an engineer keeps a dense choir clear so parts do not turn to mush.
common_mistakes: Stacking too many parts so the texture turns muddy and words vanish
Thinking more singers always sounds fuller, when spacing and voicing matter more
Ignoring low-mid buildup when many voices overlap
scenario_contexts: Thinning a dense choral pad so a lead vocal stays clear
Arranging a big final chorus with divided parts for maximum fullness
Managing low-mid mud when a large choir sings close harmony

sources: Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians

fields.definition: How clearly the words and consonants of a choir can be understood, driven by the singers' enunciation and by mic and mix choices that preserve consonant detail.
fields.plain_english: How easy it is to understand the words a choir is singing. Good diction means you can hear each word clearly, not just a wash of sound.
fields.purpose_function: Clear diction lets listeners follow the text and gives the choir crisp timing, which matters most in sacred and lyric-driven music.
fields.practical_application: An engineer protects diction by miking for consonants and avoiding heavy reverb, while the director drills crisp starts and ends of words.
common_mistakes: Drowning the words in reverb until the text turns mushy
Cutting too much high EQ, which softens consonants
Assuming diction is only the singers' job, not the engineer's
scenario_contexts: Reducing reverb send so a choir's lyrics stay clear in a mix
Recording a text-heavy anthem where every word must be understood
Adding slight presence EQ to bring out consonants

sources: Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians

fields.definition: The range and control of loud and soft levels in a choir's performance, from quiet pianissimo passages to full fortissimo, including swells and accents.
fields.plain_english: How loud or soft a choir sings, and how it moves between the two. Dynamics are the difference between a gentle whisper and a full, powerful sound.
fields.purpose_function: Dynamics give choral music its emotion and shape, and they set the recording levels an engineer must capture without clipping or noise.
fields.practical_application: An engineer sets gain and watches headroom for loud peaks, and may use gentle compression so soft and loud passages both sit well in the mix.
common_mistakes: Setting gain for soft parts, then clipping when the choir hits full volume
Over-compressing until the music loses its natural swells
Forgetting to leave headroom for loud fortissimo peaks
scenario_contexts: Setting record levels with headroom for a choir that swells from soft to loud
Riding faders to keep a quiet passage audible in a mix
Using light compression to control a wide dynamic range

sources: Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians

fields.definition: The stereo placement and spatial layout of a choir in a recording, so listeners can locate each voice section and sense the group's size and position.
fields.plain_english: Where each part of a choir seems to sit between your speakers, left to right and near to far. Good imaging lets you point to where the basses are.
fields.purpose_function: Imaging recreates the real layout of a choir, giving a mix a believable sense of space and helping voice sections stay separate and clear.
fields.practical_application: An engineer builds imaging with a main stereo mic pair and panned spot mics, arranging sections across the field to match how the choir stood.
common_mistakes: Panning spot mics so hard that sections detach from the main pair
Confusing imaging (left-right) with depth (front-back)
Ignoring phase between mics, which smears the stereo picture
scenario_contexts: Placing a main pair over a choir to capture a natural stereo image
Panning section mics to match the choir's stage layout
Checking mono compatibility so imaging does not collapse

fields.definition: How convincingly a choral recording reproduces the natural sound of a live choir, including its tone, blend, space, and depth.
fields.plain_english: How much a recording sounds like a real choir in the room with you. High realism feels live and natural, not thin or fake.
fields.purpose_function: Realism is the goal of many choral recordings, keeping the blend and hall sound so the listener feels present at the performance.
fields.practical_application: An engineer chases realism with natural mic techniques, good room capture, and restrained processing that keeps the choir sounding true to life.
common_mistakes: Over-processing until the choir sounds artificial
Adding fake reverb that fights the real hall sound
Close-miking so tightly that the natural blend is lost
scenario_contexts: Recording a choir in a fine hall to capture its natural sound
Choosing gentle processing to keep a choir sounding lifelike
Blending room mics with a main pair for a realistic sense of space

fields.definition: The balanced combination of a choir's captured tracks, such as the main pair, spot mics, and room mics, blended in level, EQ, panning, and reverb into a finished stereo recording.
fields.plain_english: The final blend of all the mics used to record a choir, set so the group sounds balanced and clear. It is like joining many photos into one good picture.
fields.purpose_function: The mix turns separate mic feeds into one cohesive choral sound, controlling tone, space, and level for the listener.
fields.practical_application: An engineer builds the mix around the main pair, adds spot mics for detail and room mics for space, then balances levels, EQ, and reverb.
common_mistakes: Leaning on spot mics so hard the main-pair blend is lost
Adding so much reverb the words and detail wash out
Mixing too bright, making sopranos harsh
scenario_contexts: Balancing main and spot mics into a finished choir recording
Blending room mics for a sense of space in a choral mix
Setting reverb and EQ so a choir sounds cohesive
